title: The 5th Corps Breaks Out: Dudakovic's Gamble at Bihac
content:
By the autumn of 1994, the Bihac pocket had endured more than two years of isolation. Cut off from the rest of government-held territory, the enclave in northwestern Bosnia was surrounded by VRS forces to the east and south, by the forces of the breakaway Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia under Fikret Abdic to the north, and by the Republic of Serbian Krajina across the Croatian border. The ARBiH 5th Corps, commanded by General Atif Dudakovic, defended a pocket that had been designated a UN safe area under UNSCR 824 but received little practical protection from that status. Supply was precarious, ammunition was rationed, and the civilian population suffered chronic shortages of food and medicine.

Dudakovic had spent months dealing with the internal threat first. Abdic's forces, supported by both the VRS and the krajina Serbs, had carved out a separatist zone in the Velika Kladusa area that divided the pocket and complicated any coherent defense. Through a series of operations in mid-1994, the 5th Corps defeated Abdic's militia and reasserted government control over the northern portion of the pocket. With the internal front secured, Dudakovic turned his attention outward.

In October 1994, the 5th Corps launched what became known as Operation Grmec. The offensive struck south and east from the pocket's perimeter, targeting VRS positions on the Grmeč mountain range — elevated terrain that had allowed Serb forces to dominate the approaches to Bihac. The assault achieved tactical surprise. VRS units in the sector, accustomed to a largely static front against a besieged and under-supplied garrison, were not positioned to absorb a concentrated offensive. ARBiH brigades advanced rapidly, capturing key positions and pushing toward Bosanska Krupa. Significant territory changed hands in a matter of days.

The success was remarkable given the 5th Corps' material disadvantages. The corps had limited heavy weapons, constrained ammunition stocks, and no prospect of reinforcement from outside the pocket. What it possessed was high morale, experienced infantry hardened by years of enclave warfare, and a commander willing to accept risk. Dudakovic concentrated his available forces against what he judged to be the weakest point in the VRS cordon and achieved the kind of local superiority that the broader ARBiH force structure rarely managed.

The VRS reaction was swift and severe. The Bosnian Serb military command, alarmed by the loss of the Grmeč mountain range and the threat to its positions in the Krajina, mobilized a counteroffensive that drew in forces from multiple corps areas. Units from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and remnants of Abdic's militia joined the response. By late November, the counterattack had pushed the 5th Corps back toward the town of Bihac itself, creating the most serious crisis the pocket had faced. The situation deteriorated to the point where the fall of the enclave appeared possible.

The Bihac crisis that followed the breakout exposed the contradictions of international policy in stark terms. NATO conducted limited air strikes against VRS positions, including the Udbina airfield in krajina Serb territory, but the strikes were too constrained to alter the military situation. UNPROFOR's presence complicated rather than facilitated decisive action, as the vulnerability of peacekeepers to hostage-taking inhibited escalation.

Dudakovic's offensive demonstrated that the ARBiH was capable of mounting effective operations even under extreme conditions of isolation and deprivation. It also demonstrated the limits of such success when the broader strategic context remained unfavourable. The 5th Corps had won a battle but triggered a crisis it could not resolve alone.
